questions.question: Agriculture contributes only 2–3 per cent of GDP. Give the arguments that show it remains vital to the South African economy.
questions.expected_answer: It feeds the population; it employs a significant share of the workforce, concentrated in rural areas with few alternatives; it supplies raw materials to agro-processing (mills, canneries, refineries, abattoirs), multiplying its true economic weight; it earns export income through citrus, wine, grapes, wool and maize; and it anchors rural settlement, slowing depopulation.

questions.question: Describe the location of the Maize Triangle and explain the factors favouring and hindering maize production there.
questions.expected_answer: The Maize Triangle spans the interior plateau across the Free State (largest producer), North West and the Mpumalanga highveld. Favouring: summer rainfall of roughly 500–800 mm in the growing season, hot long frost-free summers, deep fertile well-drained soils on gently rolling land suited to machinery, plus silos, railways, mills and research/expertise. Hindering: rainfall variability and recurring drought, hail and frost, soil degradation, rising input costs and climate change shifting rainfall patterns.

questions.question: Define food security and explain South Africa's national-versus-household paradox, with two strategies that address it.
questions.expected_answer: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active healthy life. South Africa is food secure at national level — producing enough staples or importing shortfalls — yet millions of households are food insecure because unemployment and poverty block economic access. Strategies: access-side measures like the National School Nutrition Programme (about nine million learners) and social grants; plus support for small-scale farmers, food gardens, reduced post-harvest losses and drought-tolerant cultivars.
